passage: In the government school at Ravangla, Nirmala Ma'am collected the Class 9 essays and sat on the verandah to check them. Tenzin's was, as usual, short and full of crossed-out lines. But this time she noticed something. Three weeks ago he had written only single, separate sentences. Today there were two paragraphs, and he had used "because" twice to explain his reasons. She wrote in the margin: "You joined your ideas with because. That is real progress." The next day she gave him a new task: five sentences about the monastery festival, one of them starting with "However". Not the full essay the others were doing. Tenzin read her margin note twice. That evening, for the first time, he stayed after class to ask what "however" really meant.

qa.a: "You joined your ideas with because. That is real progress."

qa.q: Why might Tenzin have read the margin note twice?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and pleased; seeing a specific improvement named made him feel his writing was actually getting better.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala Ma'am choose five sentences with 'However' instead of the full essay?
qa.a: It was a step just above what Tenzin could already do, hard enough to stretch him but small enough for him to succeed.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Ma'am feel when Tenzin stays after class to ask about 'however'?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and encouraged, seeing that naming his real progress had made Tenzin want to learn more.

passage: In a Manchester secondary school, Tariq Hassan flipped through Liam's algebra homework during the lunch break. Liam had failed the last two tests, and most of his answers were still wrong. But the teacher noticed something new: Liam had written out every step this time instead of guessing the final number, and in question 4 the first three steps were perfect before one sign slipped. At the end of class Tariq crouched beside Liam's desk. "Look here. Steps one to three, spot on. Last month you'd have skipped straight to an answer. Just this minus sign." Liam stared at the page. Tariq slid over a new sheet: six problems of the same type, each a notch harder. "Try these. Show me the steps." Liam picked up his pen before the bell had even finished.

qa.q: What new thing did Tariq notice in Liam's homework?
qa.a: Liam had written out every step this time instead of guessing the final number.

qa.q: What might Liam have been thinking as he stared at the page?
qa.a: He may have been surprised that, despite failing tests, someone had spotted real progress in his steps, which made trying feel worthwhile again.

qa.q: Why did Tariq choose six problems of the same type, each a notch harder?
qa.a: They build on exactly what Liam just showed he can do, so the next task stretches him without setting him up to fail.

qa.q: How might Tariq feel seeing Liam pick up his pen before the bell had finished?
qa.a: Tariq would likely feel encouraged and hopeful, since pointing out the three correct steps seems to have made Liam eager to try again.

passage: At the municipal swimming pool, Coach Gargi watched Neelam finish her length, gasping, the last of the under-15 group as always. Neelam hauled herself out and sat on the edge, not looking at anyone. Gargi checked her stopwatch and then her notebook. "Neelam. Come here." She held out the page. "Two weeks ago, fifty-eight seconds. Today, fifty-one. And your kick has stopped splashing. That's why." Neelam blinked at the numbers. "Seven seconds?" "Seven. Tomorrow I don't want fast. I want you to breathe every three strokes for one full length. Just that." Neelam nodded slowly. When the others left, she stayed in the shallow end practising, counting under her breath.

qa.q: What was Neelam's time two weeks ago, and what is it today?
qa.a: Two weeks ago, fifty-eight seconds; today, fifty-one.

qa.q: Why did Neelam sit on the edge not looking at anyone at first?
qa.a: Finishing last again probably made her feel ashamed and sure she wasn't improving.

qa.q: Why did Coach Gargi ask only for breathing every three strokes tomorrow?
qa.a: It is one clear, reachable skill, harder than before but doable, so Neelam can succeed and keep building.

qa.q: How does Neelam's view of herself seem to change by the end?
qa.a: Seeing the seven seconds, she stops seeing herself as simply the slowest and stays behind to practise, counting under her breath.

grounding: A swimming coach shows a struggling teenager her measurable progress and sets one hard-but-doable next goal.

passage:
Dear Lipika,
I'm writing this instead of just putting a mark, because I want you to see what I saw.
In June your essays were four lines long, with no full stops. Your essay this week, about the flooded road outside your house, is fourteen lines. You used paragraphs. You wrote 'the water was the colour of tea', and that made me stop and read it twice. You spelt 'neighbour' right every single time.
I know the marks still aren't where you want them. But you are getting better, and I can point to exactly where.
Next task, and it's a stretch: write the same flood from your neighbour's point of view. Twelve lines, one describing word in each. I think you can do it. If you get stuck halfway, come and find me at lunch.
Deepa Ma'am

qa.q: How long were Lipika's essays in June?
qa.a: Four lines long, with no full stops.

qa.q: Why does Deepa Ma'am list such specific details instead of just writing 'good'?
qa.a: Deepa Ma'am feels hopeful about Lipika's progress and wants Lipika to see real proof of it, believing visible improvement will bring back Lipika's wish to try.

qa.q: What choice about the next task makes it helpful, and why?
qa.a: Making it a stretch but doable, the same flood from the neighbour's view in twelve lines with a describing word in each, plus help at lunch; it builds on what Lipika can already do.

passage:
You want to know what worked with Anand, Elizabeth? Not a pep talk. He'd heard plenty of those.
He was failing chemistry, Class 10, sitting at the back with his hood up. First thing I did was go through his last five worksheets with a highlighter. Not for mistakes. For what he'd got right. Turned out he'd balanced every equation with two elements correctly. Every one. It was only the three-element ones that fell apart.
So I showed him. 'Look, Anand. Two elements, ten out of ten.' He actually leaned in. 'Okay, Salma Ma'am,' he said. 'Then what?'
Then I gave him one three-element equation, just one, with the first step done. He got it. Next day, two, no first step.
By March he was at 61. Not a miracle. But he stopped wearing the hood in class. I think that's when he started believing it.

qa.q: Which equations had Anand been balancing correctly?
qa.a: Every equation with two elements.

qa.q: What does Anand leaning in suggest about how he felt when Salma showed him the ten out of ten?
qa.a: It suggests surprise and a spark of hope; seeing proof that he could do part of it made trying seem worthwhile again.

qa.q: What choice did Salma make about the next tasks, and why did it work?
qa.a: She set one three-element equation with the first step done, then two without; each step was hard but doable, so Anand kept succeeding and building up.

qa.q: How might Salma Ma'am have felt when Anand stopped wearing the hood in class?
qa.a: Salma Ma'am was probably quietly encouraged, taking it as the sign that Anand had started believing in himself, which mattered more than the 61.

grounding: A teacher shows a struggling student exactly what he already does well and sets the next task just beyond it, rebuilding his wish to try.

passage: I teach English to Class 9 at the municipal school, and Uday sits in the last row. In June his essays were four lines long, with no full stops. Honestly, I nearly gave up on him. Last week he handed in a full page about his grandmother's kitchen. It was still messy, but it had paragraphs. So I did something different. Instead of just a mark, I circled three things and wrote beside each: 'Strong first line.' 'Three paragraphs, like we practised.' 'I could smell the cardamom.' And at the bottom: 'You couldn't do this in June.' I can't say what went on inside him. But he read the comments twice and put the page in his bag carefully, not crumpled. For the next essay I asked him to add one conversation, just one. The next morning he was at my desk before the bell. 'Pallavi Ma'am, how do the quote marks go?' It was the first question he'd asked all year.

qa.q: What was Uday's essay about?
qa.a: It was about his grandmother's kitchen.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel about Uday in June, and what changed?
qa.a: Pallavi felt close to giving up in June, but was encouraged by the full page and chose to name specific improvements.

qa.q: What made Pallavi's feedback effective?
qa.a: It circled three specific improvements, compared them with June, and set a next task, one conversation, that was harder but doable.

qa.q: What does Uday's question at the desk suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels more capable and wants to try, since he asks his first question of the year to get the next step right.

grounding: A teacher describes pointing out specific improvements in a weak student's essay and setting a harder but doable next task.

Monday. Kamal's algebra test came back 6 out of 25, and he shoved it under his desk. Sangeeta Ma'am, marking the pile at lunch, noticed something: on four questions he had set up the equation correctly and only slipped in the last line. Last month he hadn't set up any.
Wednesday. She called him to her table and pointed at the four setups. 'These are right. In March you couldn't do this.' Then she gave him a half-page of five problems, the first three just like those, the last two a little harder. 'Just this. Not the whole chapter.'
Friday. Kamal brought back the half-page. Four were right. He pointed at the fifth. 'I got stuck at the end. Can you show me?' He had never stayed after class before.

passage: Tarun, you say the weak ones don't want to learn. Let me tell you about Firoz, from my third year teaching science in Gorakhpur. He was fifteen and had failed every test. Other teachers called him a lost case. One day I noticed his diagram of the eye was actually neat, every label spelled right. His answer was wrong, but the drawing was good. So I wrote on it: 'Your diagram is the best in the class.' The next week he drew the ear. Also neat. I told him, 'Now write two lines explaining what one part does. Just two.' He did. Two lines became four. By the end of the year he passed, just, and he came to my desk and said, 'Madhav Sir, thank you.' I didn't do anything big, Tarun. I noticed something real, said it out loud, and gave him the next small hill.

qa.q: What was the first thing Madhav praised in Firoz's work?
qa.a: He praised his diagram of the eye, which was neat with every label spelled right.

qa.q: Why did Madhav decide to praise the diagram even though the answer was wrong?
qa.a: Madhav felt hopeful on seeing something genuinely good, and wanted Firoz to see real progress rather than another failure.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped Firoz keep trying?
qa.a: Madhav named a real strength and then set a small next step, two lines of explanation, that was hard but doable.

qa.q: How might Firoz have felt reading 'Your diagram is the best in the class'?
qa.a: Firoz, used to failing, probably felt surprised and proud, which made him want to try again.

passage:
It was the night before report cards, and the power had gone in the staff quarters. Aparna Ma'am was marking Class 9 English essays by the light of a phone torch, forty-two still to go.
Sarika's was near the bottom. Sarika, who wrote three lines and gave up. Who had failed the last two essays.
This one was a full page. The spelling was still rough. But there was a paragraph break, and a real opening sentence: “The first thing I noticed about the new bus driver was his whistle.”
Aparna Ma'am smiled in the dark. She wrote in the margin: “Your opening makes me want to read on. You used paragraphs! Next time: add one line about how you felt.”
In the morning she handed it back personally. Sarika read the comment twice, then looked up, amazed. “You noticed the paragraphs?”
“I noticed. Next essay, add the feeling line. You can do that.”

qa.q: What was the opening sentence of Sarika's essay?
qa.a: “The first thing I noticed about the new bus driver was his whistle.”

qa.q: How did Aparna Ma'am feel when she read Sarika's essay?
qa.a: She felt pleased and quietly delighted, smiling in the dark because Sarika had clearly improved.

qa.q: Why was the teacher's comment effective?
qa.a: It named specific improvements, the opening and the paragraphs, and set one next step that was hard but doable.

qa.q: How did Sarika experience the comment?
qa.a: Sarika felt amazed and encouraged that her teacher noticed the paragraphs, which makes her more willing to try again.

grounding: The passage shows a teacher noticing specific progress in a weak student's essay and setting a doable next step, rebuilding the wish to try.

passage:
Urmila had sat at the back of the Class 8 maths room in the Pune school for two terms, head down, handing in half-empty worksheets.
Amandeep Sir had noticed something. On the latest algebra sheet, she had got question 3 fully right, and in question 5 she had set up the equation correctly before getting lost.
After class he put the sheet in front of her. “Look at number 5. You wrote x plus 7 equals 19. That's exactly the hard part. Most people get stuck before that.”
Urmila frowned at the page as if it were someone else's.
“Tomorrow,” he said, “I'm giving you three problems like number 5. Not ten. Three. I think you'll get at least two.”
She got two. The next week she moved one bench forward.

qa.a: She had written x plus 7 equals 19.

qa.q: What might Amandeep Sir have felt when he noticed question 5?
qa.a: He likely felt hopeful and encouraged, seeing a real step of progress in a student who usually gave up.

qa.q: What made Amandeep Sir's approach work?
qa.a: He pointed to the exact part she did well and gave three similar problems, hard but doable, so she could see herself succeed.

qa.q: How does Urmila's view of herself change, and what shows it?
qa.a: She begins to see herself as someone who can do maths, and moving one bench forward shows her growing willingness.

passage:
“Aparna, stay back a minute.”
“Ma'am, I know, my science project is bad.”
“Actually,” Sabina Ma'am said, “look at this. Your labelled diagram of the heart. Last month you didn't label anything.”
“It's still messy.”
“Messy, yes. But every chamber is right. And here, you wrote why blood goes to the lungs. In your own words.”
Aparna looked at the page. “I just copied the book.”
“You didn't. The book says ‘oxygenation’. You wrote ‘to pick up fresh air’. That's you understanding it.”
Aparna's mouth twitched.
“For the next one, I want you to explain the kidney the same way. Just one page, your words. It'll be harder, but you've shown me you can do this.”
“One page?”
“One page.”
Aparna picked up her bag. At the door she turned. “Can I use colours?”
“Please do.”

passage:
In Class 11, I joined our school's peer-tutoring club and was paired with Vidya from Class 8. Her English teacher had written "weak" on her report. The first essay Vidya showed me was six lines, full of crossings-out. She said, "I'm hopeless," before I'd even read it.
I didn't correct everything. I looked for what was better than last time. Her second essay had a proper opening line. I pointed at it. "This sentence. Last week you didn't have one like this." She looked surprised. Then I gave her the next task: just one paragraph, with one example. Hard, but not too hard.
By December her essays were a page long. I didn't do anything magic. I just kept showing her where she'd grown and setting the next step a tiny bit higher. Watching her start to raise her hand in class was the best part of my year.
— Lakshmi

qa.a: It was six lines, full of crossings-out.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling watching Vidya raise her hand in class?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt proud and happy, calling it the best part of the year.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi's approach rebuild Vidya's wish to try?
qa.a: Lakshmi pointed out specific improvements and set each next task just a bit harder, so Vidya could see her own progress.

qa.q: How did Vidya see herself at the start?
qa.a: Vidya felt hopeless, saying so before Lakshmi had even read the essay.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9, by Nikita
Zubin has failed two physics tests this term and has started putting his head on the desk during lessons. Today I went through his last three answer sheets side by side instead of only the latest. His diagrams have improved: in August, no labels; in September, half; last week, all labelled correctly. His units are now right most of the time.
I showed him the three sheets in order. "Look at the diagrams. What changed?" He looked for a long time. "I label them now." "Every one. That's progress you made."
What I did next: I gave him one numerical problem on the same topic, a bit harder than last week's but using the method he knows. He solved it in ten minutes and asked for another. I'll keep the next tasks one step above what he can do now, and show him the sheets again at the end of the month.

qa.q: How many physics tests has Zubin failed this term?
qa.a: Zubin has failed two physics tests this term.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when laying the three sheets side by side?
qa.a: Nikita felt hopeful and encouraged, spotting real improvement Zubin himself couldn't see.

qa.q: Why did the next task help Zubin keep going?
qa.a: It was a bit harder than last week's but used a method he knew, so it was challenging yet doable, and success made him ask for more.

qa.q: How had Zubin been feeling before this lesson?
qa.a: Zubin seemed discouraged and defeated, putting his head on the desk after two failed tests.

passage:
Monday night
I'm helping Akash from Class 7 with maths at the colony study circle every evening. When we started, he got every word problem wrong and said, "I'm just stupid." Today I noticed something. He still gets the final answers wrong sometimes, but he now writes down what the question is asking before starting. Three weeks ago he never did that.
I told him exactly that: "You wrote what the question wants. That's new. That's why you got the first two right." He looked at his notebook as if it belonged to someone else.
Then I gave him a problem with two steps instead of one. Harder, but only a bit. He got it on the second try and punched the air.
I think he needed someone to show him the progress, because he couldn't see it himself.
Saurabh

qa.q: What does Akash now do before starting a problem?
qa.a: He now writes down what the question is asking before starting.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel noticing Akash's new habit?
qa.a: Saurabh felt pleased and encouraged, seeing progress that Akash hadn't noticed himself.

qa.q: Why was the two-step problem the right next task?
qa.a: It was a bit harder but still doable, so solving it on the second try gave Akash visible proof of improvement.

qa.q: How did Akash react when he got the two-step problem right?
qa.a: Akash felt proud and excited, punching the air.
